title: StackForge x Redwood — Model updates + versioning deep dive
topics: How Redwood communicates model updates today vs upcoming changelog
Model/version identifiers (model_id, version_id) and pinning behavior
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private: compatibility guarantees and rollout controls
Customer-visible release notes templates and what will/ won’t be included
Auditability: who changed what, when; immutability/retention expectations
Console mocks: changelog tab + filters + export/share links
summary: StackForge asked for a technical breakdown of how Redwood will communicate model updates to avoid surprises during rollouts and A/B tests. Redwood walked through the upcoming Model Metadata Schema v1 and changelog generator approach (registry as source of truth + signed change events), what fields will be customer-visible vs internal-only, and how pinning to a model version will work across Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Redwood shared early Console mock concepts for a Changelog tab on model/version pages, and discussed a machine-readable feed (JSON + RSS) plus API/SDK response fields/headers for resolved model_version and changelog_url. StackForge emphasized enterprise-style change management: immutable history, review workflow, and predictable deprecation timelines.
questions: If we pin a version, can it still change under us (weights, tokenizer, runtime kernels)?
Will you publish performance deltas or just ‘compatibility notes’?
Can we get an RSS or JSON feed for model updates (and filter by model)?
How do you handle corrections if a release note is wrong without losing audit history?
For Dedicated/Private, can we approve before a model becomes available in our env?
Do the release notes include deprecation timelines and replacement guidance?
next_steps: Redwood to share a one-pager on Model Metadata Schema v1 fields and customer-visible allowlist (Quentin).
Redwood to enroll StackForge in the Console changelog private beta once feature flag is ready (Chloe).
Redwood to send example JSON feed entry + proposed RSS subscription URL format (Dylan).
StackForge to provide their internal change-management requirements (retention duration, approval gates, preferred notification channel) (Marta/Aisha).
Schedule a follow-up in ~2 weeks to review beta access + sample release notes for a recent model update (Dylan).

transcript:
Meeting Header
Title: StackForge x Redwood — Model updates + versioning deep dive
Date: 2026-02-05
Time: 4:00 PM PT
Duration: 54 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Dylan Brooks, Quentin Harris, Chloe Martin
StackForge: Aisha Rahman (Platform Eng), Ben Kline (Staff Eng), Marta S. (Security/Compliance)


[00:00] Dylan Brooks: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for hopping on. This is Dylan. I’m on the platform side. Quentin’s our model catalog engineer, and Chloe runs the console backend.

[00:12] Aisha Rahman: Hey. Thanks Dylan. Yeah we wanted to go deeper than the usual demo. Specifically: how you communicate model updates, what gets changed when, and how we can avoid like… surprise behavior changes.

[00:25] Ben Kline: Yeah. We got burned by a different vendor where “same model name” was not the same model.

[00:31] Dylan Brooks: Yep, totally. That’s basically the reason this whole project exists internally.

[00:38] Dylan Brooks: Quick framing: today, we’re inconsistent. Some updates are in docs pages, sometimes a Slack message to a few accounts, sometimes runtime release notes. We’re standardizing on a model registry schema and then generating a customer-visible changelog from that.

[00:57] Marta S.: When you say “changelog”, is that like, immutable? Like we can show auditors.

[01:03] Dylan Brooks: That’s the intention. There’s a review and publish workflow, and we keep the historical record even if we have to correct something.

[01:11] Chloe Martin: And we’ll be exposing it in Console and via a feed endpoint. But we can dig into the mechanics.

[01:17] Aisha Rahman: Great. So let’s start with… identifiers. When we call the API today we pass a model string. What is the canonical thing going forward.

[01:28] Quentin Harris: Yeah. So conceptually: model_id is like the family, and version_id is the immutable served artifact. We’ll also have a display_name for humans.

[01:41] Ben Kline: “Immutable” means weights and tokenizer and everything, right?

[01:45] Quentin Harris: For the version_id, yes: weights, tokenizer revision, quantization profile, context window config. Anything that would change outputs or compatibility should trigger a new version.

[01:58] Ben Kline: Should trigger, or must trigger.

[02:02] Quentin Harris: Must, in the policy we’re writing. If it changes the served artifact, new version_id.

[02:08] Dylan Brooks: There’s nuance around runtime-level improvements, like kernel changes. That might improve latency without changing outputs. But if there’s any behavior-affecting change, new version.

[02:21] Aisha Rahman: That nuance is exactly where vendors get slippery.

[02:25] Dylan Brooks: Yep. So one piece we’re adding is compatibility notes and a “serving runtime dependency” pointer. If a runtime upgrade impacts performance for a given model/version, that can create a changelog entry too, but it’s classified as performance/runtime alignment.

[02:43] Marta S.: Are you saying you’ll publish runtime changes as model changes?

[02:47] Dylan Brooks: Not always as a new version. But as a note linked to the model version, so you can see “runtime X.Y changed throughput expectations” without pretending weights changed.

[02:58] Chloe Martin: And in Console, we’re planning to show this as entries tagged by type: new model, new version, performance update, compatibility update, deprecation.

[03:09] Ben Kline: Do you have that taxonomy already?

[03:12] Dylan Brooks: It’s being defined by product, but yes, roughly those categories.

[03:19] Aisha Rahman: Okay. Our other big thing is we do A/B tests. We’ll pin versions in the experiment, and then we need to know if anything changed during the window.

[03:32] Quentin Harris: So the plan is: when you request “model=foo” without a version, you’re basically tracking the default alias. If you request model plus version_id, that’s pinned. The response will also include the resolved model_version so you can log it.

[03:50] Ben Kline: That will be in response JSON?

[03:53] Chloe Martin: Both. We’re adding it to the response payload for OpenAI-compatible routes, and also as headers: like X-Redwood-Model-Version and X-Redwood-Changelog-URL.

[04:05] Ben Kline: Nice. That’s the kind of thing we can pipe into our traces.

[04:10] Aisha Rahman: And the changelog URL is per version?

[04:13] Chloe Martin: Per entry, and entries are tied to model_id and version_id, and also have an event_id behind the scenes.

[04:22] Marta S.: Event id like for audit logs.

[04:25] Chloe Martin: Exactly. The internal system uses a change-event stream. Customer-facing entry won’t show the actor name usually, but we retain the audit record.

[04:37] Dylan Brooks: We can talk about what’s customer-visible vs internal-only.

[04:42] Aisha Rahman: Please. Also, we’d like some performance deltas. If latency changes materially, we want to know.

[04:49] Quentin Harris: So schema v1 has performance fields, but we’re not planning to always publish numerical deltas in the release note. We might publish “expected latency improved” and link to a dashboard, depending on account tier.

[05:06] Ben Kline: Why not publish the numbers.

[05:09] Dylan Brooks: Two reasons: (1) they vary by region/hardware and workload; (2) we don’t want release notes to be a marketing benchmark war. But we can link to metrics or provide ranges.

[05:25] Aisha Rahman: That’s fair if the dashboard is stable and per environment.

[05:29] Chloe Martin: For Dedicated, it’s much easier to give you stable expected numbers.

[05:34] Ben Kline: We’re probably Dedicated anyway.

[05:37] Dylan Brooks: Right. And for Dedicated and Private, there’s also a “rollout gating” feature where your env doesn’t receive a new default alias until you approve, depending on the policy.

[05:51] Marta S.: Is that in v1.

[05:53] Dylan Brooks: It’s part of the rollout product. The changelog is the comms layer. But we’re tying them together: rollouts will reference the published changelog entry at the time of change.

[06:08] Aisha Rahman: Can you show the Console mock.

[06:10] Chloe Martin: Yeah, let me describe it since I can’t share screen recording here. On the model page, we add a “Changelog” tab. There’s a filter by date range, change type, and deployment mode. Entries show a customer-safe summary, “Impact”, “Compatibility”, “Deprecation”, and links.

[06:32] Ben Kline: Export?

[06:34] Chloe Martin: Yep, export as JSON or CSV, and also a shareable link.

[06:40] Marta S.: For our change management board, we basically need: what changed, when, and what we need to do. And proof that it won’t be altered later.

[06:52] Dylan Brooks: Totally. So we’re implementing immutability as “append-only history.” If we publish a note and it’s wrong, we publish a superseding correction entry that references the prior one, and the prior remains visible but marked superseded.

[07:12] Marta S.: That works for auditors. As long as it’s clear.

[07:17] Ben Kline: And what about deprecations. Do you guarantee a timeline.

[07:21] Quentin Harris: We have required fields: deprecation_status, sunset_date, and replacement_model (or recommended next version). Plus customer_messaging.

[07:35] Aisha Rahman: Customer messaging is a field in the schema.

[07:37] Quentin Harris: Yep, but there’s a customer-visible allowlist. Some internal notes won’t be included.

[07:44] Ben Kline: Like internal codenames.

[07:46] Quentin Harris: Exactly. We’ve had issues where people wrote internal nicknames or vendor-specific stuff. The generator only renders from approved fields.

[07:56] Dylan Brooks: Docs team has a style guide: like do/don’t language. No “we had a paging incident” type notes.

[08:06] Aisha Rahman: Okay. How do you prevent someone from editing an old note silently.

[08:12] Chloe Martin: Publish path is role-gated. Only specific roles can approve publish. And the published entry is stored as an immutable blob; edits create a new version of the entry.

[08:25] Marta S.: Do you have retention commitments.

[08:29] Dylan Brooks: We’re targeting multi-year retention, and for enterprise we can align to your requirements. The audit events have a longer retention policy than the public notes.

[08:43] Ben Kline: Can we subscribe. Like RSS.

[08:46] Chloe Martin: Yes. Plan is both RSS/Atom and JSON feed. JSON feed endpoint supports pagination and filtering by model_id, and we’re doing ETags and caching.

[09:02] Aisha Rahman: That’s important because we’ll ingest it.

[09:05] Ben Kline: The filtering semantics matter. Like, “since timestamp” and “by model”.

[09:10] Chloe Martin: Yep. We’re leaning towards “cursor + updated_since” and stable ordering by event_id, because timestamps can collide.

[09:21] Ben Kline: Good.

[09:23] Dylan Brooks: Also: we’ll expose it in API responses so you can link directly for any request.

[09:30] Aisha Rahman: Going back: if we pin version_id, does anything change under us due to runtime.

[09:37] Quentin Harris: The goal is “no behavior change.” But performance might change if the runtime improves. We’d call that out in runtime release notes and optionally in a model changelog entry as “performance update.”

[09:53] Ben Kline: But if runtime affects numerics, like slight diffs.

[09:57] Dylan Brooks: If it affects output determinism in a meaningful way, we treat it as behavior impacting and we’d cut a new version. For most models we’re not bit-for-bit deterministic anyway because GPU kernels. But we can define thresholds.

[10:15] Ben Kline: Right, fair.

[10:18] Marta S.: Another question: for Private deployments, do we get the same release notes.

[10:23] Dylan Brooks: Yes, same schema. But publication can be scoped. Like, your Private control plane can have a changelog view for what’s available in your environment.

[10:35] Chloe Martin: It’s basically the same feed, filtered by tenancy + deployment.

[10:40] Aisha Rahman: What’s the timeline for this. We’re evaluating now.

[10:45] Dylan Brooks: Console beta in the next few weeks. The schema is already being implemented in the registry. Feeds and docs integration shortly after.

[10:56] Ben Kline: What’s “few.”

[10:59] Dylan Brooks: Like, I don’t want to overpromise. But for a private beta with a handful of accounts, this quarter.

[11:09] Aisha Rahman: Okay.

[11:11] Dylan Brooks: If you’re open, we can include StackForge in the beta. You’ll get early access to the changelog tab and the feed.

[11:19] Ben Kline: Yes please.

[11:22] Marta S.: I’ll want to review the security aspects.

[11:25] Dylan Brooks: Of course.

[11:28] Chloe Martin: One detail: we’re adding RBAC. So some people can edit metadata, fewer can publish. And publishing is logged as an audit event.

[11:42] Aisha Rahman: Who typically approves.

[11:44] Dylan Brooks: Product and release engineering for customer-visible notes, plus security review for certain categories.

[11:52] Ben Kline: Like what categories.

[11:54] Dylan Brooks: Deprecations, safety/policy changes, anything that could be construed as a security implication.

[12:03] Marta S.: Safety/policy changes are big for us. We have to document them.

[12:09] Quentin Harris: Schema has “policy notes” fields. Customer note will say e.g. “updated safety filters for X content class” at a high level, not the internal detection logic.

[12:23] Ben Kline: Makes sense.

[12:25] Aisha Rahman: Can you walk through an example entry.

[12:28] Quentin Harris: Sure. Example: “Model: Redwood-Chat-7B, New version 2026-02-01.”
- Summary: “New version improves tool calling reliability and fixes JSON schema compliance in structured outputs.”
- Impact: “May change formatting for tool-call arguments; recommended to validate downstream parsing.”
- Compatibility: “OpenAI tool-calling compatible; streaming unchanged; context window 16k.”
- Performance: “No change to pricing; latency expected similar; see dashboard link.”
- Deprecation: “Prior version sunsets 2026-03-15; replacement is this version.”

[13:06] Ben Kline: That’s pretty much what we want.

[13:09] Marta S.: And it has date stamps.

[13:11] Quentin Harris: Yep, and event IDs on the backend.

[13:15] Aisha Rahman: You mentioned docs integration.

[13:18] Dylan Brooks: Docs site will have a model release notes section. It’s generated from the same published feed. So you don’t have divergence.

[13:29] Ben Kline: Good. We’ve seen docs and API disagree.

[13:33] Chloe Martin: And we’ll also expose it in Console. So docs is more like public and Console is account-scoped.

[13:42] Aisha Rahman: Okay. What’s the “source of truth” for changes.

[13:47] Dylan Brooks: Model registry + signed change events. Not git tags, not docs.

[13:55] Ben Kline: Signed.

[13:56] Dylan Brooks: Tamper evidence. We’re still finalizing details but yeah, think “event stream with immutable storage and audit log export.”

[14:08] Marta S.: This is helpful. We’ll need some written answer for our vendor questionnaire.

[14:13] Dylan Brooks: Yep. We can provide a write-up.

[14:17] Aisha Rahman: Let’s talk about what we can do today. If we onboard before this launches, how do we avoid surprises.

[14:25] Quentin Harris: Today, best practice is: always log resolved model name + region + any headers we already provide. And pin if you’re doing an A/B.

[14:36] Chloe Martin: We can also set you up on dedicated and disable automatic alias changes during your pilot.

[14:44] Ben Kline: That’s good.

[14:46] Dylan Brooks: For hosted API, we can coordinate manual comms for any planned changes during your pilot period.

[14:55] Aisha Rahman: Okay.

[15:00] (crosstalk)

[15:02] Marta S.: One more: do you have any plan to include “eval diffs” in release notes.

[15:08] Dylan Brooks: Not in v1. We can link to evaluation dashboards, but we’re not doing automated narratives like “quality improved on X.”

[15:18] Ben Kline: Fine. Links are enough.

[15:22] Aisha Rahman: I think we covered the main stuff. Can we get the schema fields list.

[15:28] Quentin Harris: Yes. I’ll send a draft list. The customer-visible subset includes identity, versioning, provenance (high-level), context window, tool/function calling compat, deployment availability, deprecation.

[15:46] Ben Kline: Provenance “high-level” means what.

[15:49] Quentin Harris: Like base model source and license info if applicable, not internal vendor contract details.

[15:57] Ben Kline: Got it.

[16:00] Chloe Martin: And we’ll send a sample feed entry: JSON fields and how pagination works.

[16:07] Dylan Brooks: Also, we can add you to the beta list. I’ll need your account ID on our side but we can handle it.

[16:14] Aisha Rahman: Great.

[16:16] Dylan Brooks: Any other questions before we wrap.

[16:19] Marta S.: Retention: you said multi-year. We’re going to ask for 7 years for audit logs.

[16:26] Dylan Brooks: For audit logs, we can align to 7 years for enterprise. For public release notes, it’ll be indefinite or at least multiple years; we’ll confirm.

[16:38] Marta S.: Okay.

[16:40] Ben Kline: And API surface: you said headers. Please make sure it’s not just docs, actually shipped.

[16:46] Chloe Martin: Yep, it’s on the implementation plan. We’ll likely ship headers first, then expand SDK response objects.

[16:55] Dylan Brooks: Alright. We’ll follow up with the docs, and schedule a check-in in two weeks.

[17:02] Aisha Rahman: Sounds good. Thanks.

[17:04] Ben Kline: Thanks.

[17:05] Marta S.: Thank you.

(Transcript continues with light scheduling chatter and ends shortly after.)
